picks.title: Breaking through AlphaFold's limits to predict how proteins change shape
picks.excerpt: Researchers at Japan's Institute for Molecular Science built AF3-ReD, which adds a repulsive force between predicted structures so AlphaFold3 stops collapsing to one conformation. It recovered open, closed and intermediate states of ATP synthase that standard AlphaFold3 misses.
picks.rationale: AlphaFold3's single-shape blind spot is the field's best-known limitation, and AF3-ReD is a simple, reusable fix that changes how structural biologists run predictions tomorrow.

picks.title: Six unusual structures identified at Earth's core-mantle boundary with the help of deep learning
picks.excerpt: A neural network sifted more than 2 million seismic recordings from 1990-2024 and flagged about 174,929 PKP precursor signals, roughly ten times all previous global datasets combined. The haul revealed six continuous belts of deep-mantle irregularities that earlier work saw only as scattered points.
picks.rationale: A ten-fold jump in usable seismic signals turns scattered dots into six continuous belts — a vivid case of AI finding new planetary structure, not just speeding up old work.

picks.title: These smart bricks know what object they make up
picks.excerpt: Researchers built modular bricks that collectively infer the shape they have been assembled into — boat, chair or guitar — by sharing local sensor signals. The work pushes machine learning out of the server and into the material itself.
picks.rationale: Computation living inside the material rather than a server is an idea any reader can picture, and it is the most tangible physical-AI result in the pool.

picks.title: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
picks.excerpt: Google reports a real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system that runs hypothesis generation, experiment design and manuscript writing end to end. The paper moves the AI co-scientist claim from in-silico demos to laboratory outcomes.
picks.rationale: The AI co-scientist claim finally comes with wet-lab outcomes instead of in-silico demos — the single most consequential AI-for-science report in the pool.

picks.title: Brain activity patterns could help sharpen LLM deductive reasoning
picks.excerpt: Peking and Tsinghua University teams found LLM internal activity during reasoning partly aligns with human brain regions used for logical problem solving. Their brain-guided training framework used imaging data to push deductive reasoning past what text-only training achieved.
picks.rationale: Using human brain imaging as a training signal beats text-only training on deduction — a concrete neuroscience-to-AI transfer, and the pool's only cognitive-science angle.
